title: The slowest expert sets the pace
subtitle: Implement dispatch and combine, then make skew your adversary.
outcomes: Implement top-k dispatch and weighted combine without changing model semantics.
Predict when communication or expert imbalance controls latency.
Evaluate replication with migration cost and changing workloads.
body:
A mixture-of-experts layer exchanges dense, predictable work for sparse, irregular work. A router chooses a small subset of experts for each token, but the machine must still store those experts, move activations to their owners, execute differently sized matrix multiplications, and restore the original token order. Counting only activated parameters misses most of the systems problem. [Mixtral](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04088) is a useful concrete routing architecture; [DeepEP](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP) provides a communication implementation to study after building your own reference.

## Preserve the logical expert computation

For token vector $x_t$, let $S_t$ contain the selected logical experts and $g_{t,e}$ their normalized weights. The layer computes

$$y_t=\sum_{e\in S_t}g_{t,e}f_e(x_t).$$

A logical expert is part of the model. A physical expert is a particular copy placed on a device. Replicating a logical expert can preserve this expression; replacing it with a different, less busy expert generally cannot. This distinction determines which load balancing interventions are numerical optimizations and which require model-quality evaluation.

## Dispatch is a gather; combine is a reduction

Build the execution path in five explicit stages. Compute routing indices and weights. Count assignments per destination. Pack token vectors with their original token index and expert slot. Execute each expert on its gathered rows. Return and reduce the weighted outputs by original token index. A token routed to two experts creates two assignments, so a permutation alone is insufficient: the inverse operation includes a reduction. Use a simple reference first:

```python
out = zeros_like(tokens)
for token_id, expert_id, weight in assignments:
    out[token_id] += weight * experts[expert_id](tokens[token_id])
```

Your optimized implementation must agree with this reference under a stated floating-point tolerance. Test repeated experts across tokens, empty expert batches, noncontiguous token IDs, and tokens whose selected experts live on different devices. Do not silently drop assignments when an expert exceeds a convenient buffer size. Capacity clipping changes outputs unless that behavior is explicitly part of the model contract.

## Put a byte budget on communication

Now derive a traffic estimate. With $N$ tokens, top-$k$ routing, hidden width $d$, and $b$ bytes per activation element, naive dispatch plus return moves approximately $2Nkd b$ bytes globally, before metadata and protocol overhead. Some assignments stay local; implementations can avoid redundant sends when several selected experts share a destination. Thus this is a logical traffic model, not a claim about NIC counters. For $N=4096$, $k=2$, $d=4096$, and BF16 activations, the model gives $134{,}217{,}728$ bytes, or 128 MiB. At an assumed aggregate effective payload rate of 100 GB/s, moving that amount alone takes about 1.34 ms. Using a single link's bandwidth as the denominator for whole-cluster traffic would be an invalid comparison.

## Measure the slowest rank

The compute bottleneck is equally easy to hide. Suppose four ranks receive 4096, 2048, 1024, and 1024 assignments. The average is 2048, but the slowest rank receives twice that. Define imbalance $I=\max_r n_r/\operatorname{mean}_r n_r$. Here $I=2$. If execution cost is approximately linear in assignment count and all other costs vanish, perfect balancing can provide at most a twofold improvement for this stage. Real GEMM efficiency depends on shape, so doubling rows need not exactly double time. Record both assignment counts and measured rank completion times.

## Make replication repay its cost

Replication spends memory to reduce the maximum load. If the hottest expert receives 3000 assignments and has two copies, ideal splitting produces 1500 per copy. That arithmetic assumes equal device speed, uncongested routing, and enough free capacity elsewhere. A copy placed beside another hot expert may leave rank-level skew unchanged. A sensible placement objective therefore minimizes predicted maximum rank service time, subject to memory and migration constraints, rather than merely equalizing expert counts.

Rebalancing also has a break-even horizon. If moving weights costs 40 ms and saves 0.2 ms per subsequent step, the new placement needs more than 200 useful steps to repay migration. When workload phases change every 50 steps, an aggressive controller may perpetually chase yesterday's hot expert. Add hysteresis, a minimum residency period, and a migration budget. Keep an oracle placement as an upper bound; it is not a deployable baseline because it knows future traffic.

## Test the critical path under changing traffic

The supplied MoE lab is a CPU teaching simulation of routing load. Extend it into a real dispatch/combine implementation only when you have the devices and communication library. For the simulation, sweep uniform, skewed, and phase-changing assignments using fixed seeds. Report imbalance before and after placement, predicted critical-path work, and migration volume. For the accelerator extension, measure dispatch, expert GEMM, combine, and exposed communication separately, then measure the entire layer without diagnostic synchronization. Report p50 and p99 step latency, per-rank loads, memory, and all assignment losses, which should be zero.

A trace can show concurrent communication and compute without proving successful overlap. The overlap helps only if it shortens the layer's critical path; it can also steal memory bandwidth or execution resources from the GEMMs. Compare serial and overlapped variants at identical routes and batch shapes. Finish the week with one case where replication wins and one where it loses. The general lesson is to treat sparse model structure as a changing scheduling problem constrained by exact token semantics, not as an automatic reduction in serving cost.

exercises.title: Reconstruct the inverse dispatch
exercises.prompt: Three tokens select experts (0,1), (1,2), (0,2) with weights (0.7,0.3), (0.4,0.6), (0.2,0.8). Design metadata sufficient to combine any arrival order.

exercises.title: Price a replica
exercises.prompt: An expert migration costs 75 ms. It reduces each layer step from 2.8 ms to 2.3 ms for 120 steps before a traffic phase changes. Is it worthwhile?
exercises.hint: Compare accumulated savings with the one-time cost.
exercises.solution: Savings are 120 × 0.5 = 60 ms, below the 75 ms migration cost. Net latency increases 15 ms. Break-even is 150 steps; a strict improvement requires more than 150, ignoring added memory and routing overhead.

exercises.title: Separate model routing from physical placement
exercises.prompt: Propose an experiment comparing hot-expert replication with routing to a less busy different expert.
exercises.hint: One changes execution placement; the other changes the function.
exercises.solution: Hold tokens, logical router decisions, and weights fixed for the replication experiment; compare outputs to the unreplicated reference and latency under the same trace. The alternative-expert experiment must separately measure model quality because f_a(x) generally differs from f_b(x). Do not mix its throughput into an exact-optimization claim.

quiz.question: Four ranks receive [100,100,100,500] assignments. What is the imbalance ratio?
quiz.explanation: The mean load is (100+100+100+500)/4 = 200 assignments. Dividing the maximum, 500, by that mean gives 2.5; dividing by the smallest rank would measure something different.

quiz.question: Which intervention preserves the logical MoE function in principle?
options: Run the chosen expert on an identical physical replica
Replace the busiest expert with the next-best router score
Normalize weights after deleting one route
quiz.explanation: An identical physical replica evaluates the same logical expert function, provided routing weights and combine semantics are preserved. Substituting another expert or dropping a route changes the model computation.

quiz.question: Why can expert counts look balanced while ranks are imbalanced?
options: Several busy experts may share one rank
quiz.explanation: Ranks execute the sum of work assigned to their resident experts. Several individually busy experts can share one rank, so balancing expert totals alone does not balance the device critical path.

quiz.question: A 30 ms migration saves 0.1 ms per step. When is latency improved?
quiz.explanation: The accumulated saving is 0.1 ms times the number of useful steps. At 300 steps it only repays the 30 ms move; a strict improvement requires more than 300 steps and assumes no additional overhead.

quiz.question: Which result best demonstrates useful communication overlap?
options: Two colored bars overlap in a trace
End-to-end layer time falls at identical routing and correctness
quiz.explanation: Useful overlap reduces the time until the entire layer finishes under the same routes, shapes, and correctness contract. Concurrent trace bars alone do not prove a shorter critical path and may hide resource contention.

title: When prefill and decode should separate
subtitle: A transfer budget, two queues, and a fair comparison.
outcomes: Derive a KV transfer lower bound from the actual cache representation.
Compare colocated and separated service under equal resources.
Design handoff ownership and failure recovery.
body:
Prefill and decode ask different things of a GPU. A long prompt supplies many token rows at once; a decode iteration supplies a small number of new rows while reading historical state. Sharing devices lets an engine exploit spare capacity, but one phase can disrupt the other's deadlines. Separating the phases gives independent scheduling and placement at the cost of moving state and managing another queue. [DistServe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670) frames this as a goodput problem under both first-token and inter-token constraints. Treat its architecture as a hypothesis whose advantage depends on workload and interconnect.

## Draw the handoff timeline

Start with a complete timeline. A request arrives, waits for prefill, executes prefill, transfers its cache, waits for decode admission, and produces output. For a first token emitted by the decode side, an illustrative decomposition is

$$T_{\mathrm{first}}=Q_P+P+X_{KV}+Q_D+D_1.$$

An engine may emit the first token on the prefill worker, so instrument the actual boundary rather than imposing this formula blindly. A user can receive token one promptly and then wait a long time for token two while handoff occurs. Report the largest early token gap as well as time to first token. Otherwise an implementation can appear responsive while moving its delay just beyond the chosen metric.

## Derive the actual KV payload

The transfer size comes from the cache representation, not the parameter count. For ordinary grouped-query attention with $L$ layers, $h_{kv}$ key/value heads, head width $d_h$, $s$ cached positions, and $b$ bytes per scalar,

$$M_{KV}=2Lh_{kv}d_hsb.$$

The factor two represents keys and values. With 32 layers, eight KV heads, width 128, 8192 positions, and BF16 storage, the cache occupies 1,073,741,824 bytes: exactly 1 GiB before padding and metadata. A 25 GB/s effective link needs at least 42.95 ms for that payload; a 100 GB/s link needs 10.74 ms. Both are optimistic bounds. Include serialization, connection setup, memory registration, source/destination copies, and any layout conversion actually present.

Compression changes this calculation. A latent cache may store substantially fewer elements; quantized state may add scale metadata; sliding-window layers retain only a suffix. Tensor and context parallel layouts can require redistribution. Write a cache inventory per layer type before estimating network load. Never use dense-attention cache bytes to claim a transfer bottleneck for a model with a compressed representation. Conversely, allocating a compressed cache does not establish that your transfer implementation sends the compressed form.

## Find the latency crossover

Disaggregation is worthwhile when avoided interference and better resource specialization exceed transfer and coordination costs at the desired operating point. Consider a deliberately simplified example: colocation produces 75 ms p95 inter-token gaps during long prompts. Separation reduces these to 30 ms, but adds 25 ms to a 300 ms first-token target. If prefill plus queues previously consumed 250 ms, that request still fits the target at 275 ms. If it consumed 290 ms, the same change fails first-token service. One global throughput number cannot represent both cases.

## Balance two service pools

Resource allocation is a tandem-queue problem. Suppose a prefill worker can sustainably admit 4 requests/s for the chosen prompt mix, while a decode worker can complete 2 requests/s for the chosen output mix. One prefill worker feeding one decode worker does not form a 4 requests/s system: decode is the bottleneck. A 1:2 worker ratio nominally balances rates, but variance and SLO headroom still matter. Those rates are workload dependent, especially with prefix hits and heavy-tailed outputs. Measure service demand distributions rather than assuming every request consumes equal work.

## Transfer ownership, not just bytes

State transfer needs a protocol. Assign a request generation ID and a cache version; reserve destination capacity before committing ownership; acknowledge complete receipt; only then permit source reclamation. Partial transfer must not expose a half-populated cache to decode. Cancellation must reach both workers. If a worker dies after sending tokens, a retry must not append an unrelated second continuation to the same stream. A robust implementation distinguishes replayable prefill work, committed output, and uncommitted speculative state.

## Run an equal-resource experiment

The reference scheduler lab models admission and queueing on the CPU. This week you extend its event model with separate prefill/decode servers and an explicit transfer delay; the supplied script does not claim to run a disaggregated GPU service. First verify zero-transfer cases against a hand-calculated timeline. Then sweep prompt length, output length, cache-hit fraction, link rate, and arrival burstiness. Keep total GPU count fixed across the comparison and include a tuned colocated baseline with chunked prefill. Comparing an untuned single device against several specialized workers confounds the architectural conclusion.

A measurement subtlety matters here: percentiles do not generally add. Adding the p95 transfer time to the p95 prefill time is not necessarily the p95 total, because the slow cases may occur on different requests or be correlated. Join stage records by request ID and compute end-to-end percentiles from the summed per-request timelines. Use component percentiles for diagnosis, not as an unjustified service-level guarantee.

For hardware work, log every handoff with request ID, bytes, source/destination, start/end timestamps, and cache ownership transitions. Measure per-stage queues, GPU utilization, network payload, first-token latency, token gaps, completion latency, and SLO-qualified goodput. Include failed and rejected requests in the denominator. Add a transfer interruption test and verify eventual reclamation. The experiment succeeds when it maps a crossover region: where separation helps, where colocation wins, and which measured term explains that boundary.

exercises.title: Compute the transfer floor
exercises.prompt: A cache has 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head width 128, 4096 positions, and 2-byte elements. Compute payload and a lower bound at 50 GB/s.
exercises.hint: Use decimal bandwidth and keep bytes until the final division.
exercises.solution: 2×40×8×128×4096×2 = 671,088,640 bytes = 640 MiB. Divide by 50×10^9 bytes/s to obtain 0.0134218 s, or 13.42 ms. This excludes overhead and contention.

exercises.title: Find the bottleneck ratio
exercises.prompt: Prefill capacity is 6 requests/s/worker; decode capacity is 1.5 requests/s/worker. With ten identical-cost workers, choose an integer allocation maximizing ideal steady-state throughput.
exercises.hint: Compare min(6P,1.5D) subject to P+D=10.
exercises.solution: P=2,D=8 gives min(12,12)=12 requests/s. P=1 gives 6; P=3 gives 10.5. The balanced allocation is optimal under these simplified constant-rate assumptions; real latency SLOs require spare capacity.

exercises.title: Close the handoff race
exercises.prompt: The source frees KV immediately after starting an asynchronous transfer. Identify the bug and design a cancellation-safe protocol.
exercises.hint: Sending a transfer is not the same as the destination owning valid state.
exercises.solution: Keep source references until destination acknowledges a complete versioned cache. Reserve target memory first. On cancellation, mark the generation cancelled, stop decode admission, then release each side only after transfer completion or abort is confirmed. Use idempotent release and generation IDs to reject stale acknowledgements.

quiz.question: What must be held fixed for a fair architecture comparison?
options: Total resources, workload, quality, and SLO definition
quiz.explanation: Keep hardware resources, offered requests, quality requirements, and SLO definitions matched. Otherwise an apparent architectural gain may come from extra devices, easier requests, or weaker service requirements.

quiz.question: A prefill worker serves 5 req/s and a decode worker 2 req/s. One of each sustains at most:
quiz.explanation: Each admitted request must pass through both stages. The decode worker can finish only two requests per second, so a faster prefill worker merely creates a growing downstream queue above that rate.

quiz.question: Which event permits freeing source KV?
options: Destination acknowledges the complete valid cache under the handoff protocol
quiz.explanation: The source must retain valid state until the destination has acknowledged complete receipt under the ownership protocol. Enqueueing a transfer proves neither completion nor that cancellation was handled.

quiz.question: Why can TTFT conceal a handoff regression?
options: Token one may be emitted before a long pause during transfer
quiz.explanation: An implementation may emit token one on the prefill worker before moving KV. TTFT can therefore remain low while token two arrives after a long transfer pause; inspect the early inter-token gap as well.

quiz.question: Which quantity is the correct basis for KV transfer bytes?
quiz.explanation: Transfer size follows the tensors actually stored and sent, including head counts, latent compression, windows, precision, padding, and metadata. Total parameter count describes weights, which are a different object.

title: Build a service that survives success
subtitle: Route by work, reject overload early, and price useful output.
outcomes: Design admission control using predicted work and memory.
Prevent retry amplification and reclaim cancelled state.
Compare cost per successful SLO-qualified request.
body:
A serving system that performs well only below saturation is unfinished. Inference requests vary enormously in prompt size, output length, cache reuse, and modality cost. Ten short cached requests may be cheaper than one uncached document. Routing by queue length alone ignores that difference. [Google's overload chapter](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/) explains why query rate is often a poor resource proxy; translate that insight into token work, cache occupancy, and deadlines for your engine.

## Route by work and cache benefit

Construct a predicted completion cost for each candidate replica. A simple score is queued service time plus estimated new service time, with penalties for insufficient KV headroom and a benefit for reusable prefixes. This is a policy model, not a physical law. Fit service estimates from observed prompt/output buckets, track residuals, and use conservative quantiles near deadlines. A cache-aware router can reduce repeated prefill while concentrating traffic on a hot replica, so cache affinity must compete against queue delay.

Consider two replicas. A has 20 ms of queued work and can prefill a request in 10 ms because its prefix is cached. B has no queue but needs 50 ms for full prefill. A is the better first-token choice at a predicted 30 ms. If A's queue grows to 80 ms, B becomes preferable. The crossover is explicit: send to A only while its additional queueing stays below the 40 ms cache benefit, assuming decode capacity and memory are otherwise comparable. Measure the hit benefit; a nominal prefix hit may still require layout work or cache transfer.

## Understand the cost of lost headroom

Queueing explodes near capacity. In an illustrative M/M/1 model with arrival rate $\lambda$ and service rate $\mu$, mean response time is

$$E[T]=\frac{1}{\mu-\lambda}.$$

At $\mu=100$ requests/s and $\lambda=80$, the mean is 50 ms; at $\lambda=95$, it is 200 ms. This model assumes Poisson arrivals and exponential service on one server, so it does not predict real continuous-batching latency directly. Its useful lesson is the sensitivity to headroom. For real inference, replay measured arrivals and service demands, including bursts and long outputs, instead of fitting a single average and declaring the queue solved.

## Admit work before spending resources

Admission control should happen before expensive irreversible work. Check queue budget, predicted deadline feasibility, and cache reservation. If admission is impossible, reject quickly with a retry policy that does not amplify load. Once admitted, enforce output limits and cancellation promptly. A cancelled stream that continues generating invisibly wastes compute and may hold the exact KV pages needed by successful requests. Track reclaimed bytes and time from cancellation to reclamation; closing an HTTP connection is not proof that device work stopped.

## Break the retry feedback loop

Retries create positive feedback. Suppose original traffic is 80 requests/s and each failed attempt retries independently with probability $r=0.25$. With no limit, the expected attempts per request are $1/(1-r)=1.333$, producing about 106.7 attempts/s. A 100 attempts/s system can therefore be overloaded by a demand level that originally fit. [The cascading-failures chapter](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/) motivates bounded retries, backoff, jitter, and explicit retry budgets. Inference additionally needs stream-aware recovery: replaying a request after partial output can duplicate tokens or branch its continuation.

Design failure recovery around committed state. Give every logical request an idempotency key and every execution attempt a generation ID. Track which tokens have been delivered, which KV version corresponds to them, and whether exact continuation is supported. If exact state recovery is unavailable, return an explicit failure or a clearly new attempt; do not silently stitch two incompatible generations together. Simulate worker death before prefill, during handoff, and after several output tokens. Verify that orphaned reservations eventually disappear.

## Price useful completions

Cost should count useful work. Define $G$ as completed requests meeting both latency and quality requirements during a wall-clock interval, and $C$ as all infrastructure cost during that same interval. Then cost per good request is $C/G$. If deployment A costs an illustrative $12/hour and delivers 600 good requests/hour, its cost is $0.02 each. B costs $18/hour and delivers 1200, so its cost is $0.015 each. These are invented accounting examples, not current cloud prices. Include idle replicas, failed attempts, CPU, networking, and storage when they are material.

Do not let a high rejection rate manufacture an attractive tail latency. Report offered load, accepted load, completion rate, timeout rate, rejection rate, and goodput together. A service that accepts one easy request and rejects the rest can have excellent p99 latency with terrible utility. Define eligibility and SLOs before running the benchmark, stratify by workload class, and preserve the same offered trace for all policies.

## Stress the service until it recovers

This week's CPU scheduler extension adds bounded queues, work-based routing, cache-affinity scores, cancellation, and retry budgets. Compare round-robin, shortest queue, and predicted least work. Inject a fivefold arrival burst and remove one replica halfway through a run. Report recovery time and whether queue length returns to baseline. The underlying fix for overload is a controlled admission boundary backed by honest work accounting. Autoscaling can add capacity later, but it cannot rescue already accumulated stale work instantaneously.

exercises.title: Choose a cache-aware destination
exercises.prompt: Replica A has 65 ms queued work and a 15 ms cached prefill. Replica B has 10 ms queued and a 60 ms full prefill. Which wins, ignoring decode differences?
exercises.hint: Add queue and service cost.
exercises.solution: A predicts 80 ms; B predicts 70 ms, so B wins despite missing the prefix. Cache affinity is worthwhile only if saved service exceeds extra waiting.

exercises.title: Bound retry amplification
exercises.prompt: Original demand is 120 requests/s. Each attempt retries with probability 0.2, with at most two retries. Compute expected attempts/s.
exercises.hint: Use the finite geometric sum 1+r+r².
exercises.solution: Expected attempts per original request are 1+0.2+0.04=1.24. Attempt load is 148.8/s. A server able to execute 140/s will still overload; backoff changes timing but does not erase this expected work.

exercises.title: Audit a misleading cost claim
exercises.prompt: A costs $24/hour and produces 2400 responses, 60% satisfying SLOs. B costs $30/hour and produces 2100, 95% satisfying SLOs. Compare cost per good response.
exercises.hint: Use the successful counts rather than raw output.
exercises.solution: A has 1440 good responses and costs $0.01667 each. B has 1995 good responses and costs $0.01504 each. B is cheaper per useful result despite greater hourly cost and fewer total responses. Keep quality thresholds and request mix identical.

quiz.question: Which routing signal is most useful for heterogeneous prompts?
options: Predicted queued service demand with memory and cache context
quiz.explanation: Queued service demand estimates how long the new request will wait and execute. Memory availability and cache reuse can change that estimate substantially, even when replicas have the same number of requests.

quiz.question: Why should rejected requests appear in the report?
options: Otherwise dropping hard work can masquerade as better service
quiz.explanation: Without offered-load outcomes, a service can improve its latency chart simply by rejecting difficult requests. Reporting rejections together with qualifying completions reveals whether users actually receive more useful service.

quiz.question: What is the unbounded expected retry multiplier at r=0.1?
quiz.explanation: With independent retry probability r, expected attempts are the geometric sum 1+r+r²+… = 1/(1−r). At r=0.1 this is about 1.111 attempts per original request; a finite retry cap changes the sum.

quiz.question: What demonstrates cancellation completed?
options: Compute/state ownership is terminated and reservations are reclaimed
quiz.explanation: A closed connection does not guarantee that scheduled device work or KV reservations have stopped. Completion of cancellation requires the execution and ownership protocol to terminate work and reclaim its resources.

quiz.question: Which cost denominator matches a user-facing serving objective?
options: SLO- and quality-qualified completions over the billed interval
quiz.explanation: Cost per good request divides all relevant interval cost by completions satisfying the declared latency and quality contract. Raw tokens or accepted requests can include failures, wasted work, and unusable output.

title: Guess ahead without changing the distribution
subtitle: Acceptance is probability mass accounting, not a confidence threshold.
outcomes: Derive the acceptance and residual distributions.
Predict when drafting repays its extra computation.
Test sampling correctness separately from speed and same-seed identity.
body:
Imagine paying to fetch a large book from a distant shelf every time you read one word. Once the book is open, checking several proposed words can be relatively cheap. Speculative decoding exploits a similar asymmetry: an inexpensive draft proposes several tokens, and the target scores those positions together. The hard part is not guessing well. It is recovering the target distribution when the guess is wrong. The original papers by [Leviathan and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192) and [Chen and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01318) establish exact distribution-preserving sampling schemes under their numerical assumptions.

## Acceptance keeps the overlapping probability mass

Let $p(x)$ be the target's next-token distribution and $q(x)$ the draft's distribution at the same prefix. Draw $x\sim q$ and accept it with probability

$$a(x)=\min\left(1,\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right).$$

Only draft-supported tokens are proposed, so division by zero is not needed for a sampled token in exact arithmetic. Accepted mass for token $x$ is $q(x)a(x)=\min(p(x),q(x))$. This is the overlap between two probability histograms. Rejected mass must be placed where the target has more probability than the draft. Therefore, after rejection, draw from

$$r(x)=\frac{\max(p(x)-q(x),0)}{\sum_z\max(p(z)-q(z),0)}.$$

The denominator is the rejection probability. Multiplying the residual distribution by that probability restores exactly the missing target mass, so accepted plus corrected mass equals $p$. If the distributions match perfectly, rejection never occurs and the zero residual denominator is an unreachable branch, not permission to divide by zero.

## Repair a three-token distribution by hand

Work through three tokens. Let $p=(0.5,0.3,0.2)$ and $q=(0.2,0.5,0.3)$. Acceptance probabilities are $(1,0.6,2/3)$. The accepted mass is $(0.2,0.3,0.2)$, totaling 0.7. Rejection occurs with probability 0.3, and the residual is $(1,0,0)$. Final mass is therefore $(0.5,0.3,0.2)$. An intuitive but wrong correction samples directly from $p$ after rejection; that would produce $(0.35,0.39,0.26)$. Even a plausible-looking language sample can conceal this systematic bias.

## Extend the argument to a draft block

For a draft block of length $\gamma$, target verification evaluates the relevant conditional distributions in parallel with causal masking. Walk left to right, accepting until the first rejection. At that position, sample the residual token and discard the unused draft suffix. If every draft token is accepted, sample one additional token from the target distribution after the full draft. The bonus token matters for both correctness bookkeeping and the speed model. Cache entries for rejected positions must be rolled back before the next iteration.

A compact teaching implementation looks like this:

```python
for i, proposed in enumerate(draft_tokens):
    if uniform() < min(1.0, p[i][proposed] / q[i][proposed]):
        emit(proposed)
    else:
        residual = positive_part(p[i] - q[i])
        emit(sample(normalize(residual)))
        rollback_after(i)
        break
else:
    emit(sample(p_after_draft))
```

Every distribution in this code must include the intended temperature, masking, and sampling transformations. Applying top-p to the target in one path and forgetting it in another defines different target processes. The target distribution is the one after the declared decoding rules, not necessarily the raw softmax. Grammar constraints, stop conditions, and tokenizer compatibility deserve explicit tests.

## Calculate expected progress and speed

For intuition about speed, assume every conditional acceptance has the same independent rate $\alpha$. The expected emitted tokens per verification round are

$$E[K]=1+\alpha+\cdots+\alpha^\gamma=\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}.$$

This is a toy model: real acceptance varies with context and position. At $\alpha=0.8$ and $\gamma=4$, $E[K]=3.3616$. If four draft steps cost 8 ms, verification costs 12 ms, and bookkeeping costs 1 ms, the round costs 21 ms, or about 6.25 ms per emitted token. Against a 10 ms target-only decode step, predicted speedup is 1.60. At $\alpha=0.3$, expected output falls to 1.4251 and the same method takes 14.74 ms per token: a slowdown.

## Know when good guesses still lose

High batch occupancy changes the bargain. Target verification may already be compute constrained; extra draft positions increase FLOPs, and draft KV consumes memory that could otherwise hold more requests. Optimizing single-request latency can reduce service goodput. Sweep draft length, batch occupancy, prompt length, and workload type, and report accepted tokens per target call alongside wall time and memory. Separate draft cost, target verification, synchronization, and rollback.

You can connect acceptance to a familiar statistical distance. For one fixed prefix, total accepted mass is $\sum_x\min(p(x),q(x))=1-\operatorname{TV}(p,q)$, where $\operatorname{TV}(p,q)=\tfrac12\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|$. This explains why draft accuracy measured as next-token top-1 agreement is an incomplete predictor: two drafts can choose the same argmax yet assign very different probability mass elsewhere. Construct such a pair in the lab and compare acceptance. Conversely, optimizing acceptance alone can select an expensive draft whose extra latency erases its statistical advantage. Treat distribution overlap and draft execution cost as separate axes before choosing a draft model or block length.

## Test the sampling contract

The supplied CPU lab tests the probability mechanism; it does not benchmark an accelerator or reproduce any published speedup. Use a tiny vocabulary to compare empirical output frequencies with known $p$, then use a conditional two-step model to detect incorrect prefix handling. Add a deliberately wrong rejection branch and ensure your test catches it. Same random seed does not imply identical sampled text across algorithms because they consume randomness differently. Distributional equivalence, greedy-token equivalence, and bitwise repeatability are three different contracts. Finish by stating exactly which one your implementation satisfies and by demonstrating a workload where speculation should be disabled.

quiz.question: After rejecting a proposal, which distribution restores exactness?
quiz.explanation: Accepted proposals already supply min(p,q) probability mass to each token. The residual must supply exactly the remaining positive part of p−q; sampling directly from p would add mass to tokens already fully represented.

quiz.question: What is E[K] for alpha=0.5 and gamma=2 under the toy model?
quiz.explanation: The round emits at least one token, a second when the first proposal is accepted, and a third when both are accepted. Under the constant independent-rate model this gives 1+0.5+0.25 = 1.75.

quiz.question: Same seed gives different sampled text. What follows?
options: No distributional conclusion follows from this alone
quiz.explanation: A seed identifies a random stream, but two algorithms can consume that stream in different orders. Distributional correctness requires a proof and appropriate sampling tests, not identical text for one shared seed.

quiz.question: Which cache operation is necessary after the first rejection?
options: Keep all proposed state as committed
Discard or invalidate the rejected suffix before continuation
quiz.explanation: KV entries after the rejection were computed from a prefix that was never accepted. They must be discarded or invalidated before continuation; otherwise later target scores condition on the wrong history.

quiz.question: Why can higher acceptance still fail to improve serving goodput?
options: Acceptance has no relation to speed
Draft/verification cost and memory can outweigh saved iterations
The bonus token is always incorrect
quiz.explanation: Acceptance measures statistical overlap, while goodput also depends on draft latency, verification work, synchronization, and memory consumed. A more accurate but expensive draft can lower useful service throughput.

title: Spend bits where they buy behavior
subtitle: Quantization is a joint numerical, kernel, and evaluation problem.
outcomes: Derive quantization error and metadata overhead.
Distinguish representation savings from kernel speed.
Evaluate behavior on held-out workloads with uncertainty.
body:
A lower bit width is a smaller container, not an automatic faster program. The machine may need to unpack values, load scales, convert formats, and run a kernel whose tiling is poor for your shapes. Meanwhile a small perturbation in weights can move a near-tied logit across a decision boundary. The inference engineer must connect three questions: what information is discarded, how the hardware consumes the representation, and which user-visible behaviors change.

## Locate the rounding and clipping error

Begin with symmetric integer quantization. For positive scale $s$ and integer range $[-Q,Q]$, encode $w$ as $q=\operatorname{clip}(\operatorname{round}(w/s),-Q,Q)$ and reconstruct $\hat w=sq$. Without clipping, nearest rounding gives $|w-\hat w|\le s/2$. With clipping, that bound no longer applies to outliers. For $Q=7$ and a group's maximum magnitude 1.4, choose $s=0.2$. Values 0.31 and −0.94 reconstruct as 0.4 and −1.0, with errors 0.09 and 0.06. An unanticipated value 2.0 clips to 1.4, producing error 0.6. Calibration range therefore matters.

## Follow error through the activation vector

The relevant linear-layer error is not simply weight error. If $y=Wx$ and $\hat W=W+\Delta W$, then

$$\Delta y=\Delta W x,\qquad \|\Delta y\|\le\|\Delta W\|\|x\|.$$

The norm bound is conservative, but it explains why activation distribution matters. An error aligned with a large input channel can dominate one aligned with a rarely active channel. [AWQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978) uses activation information to protect important weight channels. [SmoothQuant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10438) redistributes scaling difficulty between weights and activations through an equivalent transformation before quantization. Read these as concrete strategies, not guarantees for arbitrary models or domains.

A useful identity makes the scaling idea tangible. Let $D$ be an invertible diagonal matrix. Then $Wx=(WD)(D^{-1}x)$. Before rounding, this changes no output. After rounding, different choices of $D$ redistribute error. Scaling a large activation down may require scaling a weight column up, so there is a tradeoff rather than free accuracy. Test transformations in full precision first: a transpose or channel-axis mistake can produce an apparently sophisticated quantizer that is simply wrong.

## Count payload, scales, and format costs

Count storage honestly. Four-bit values require half a byte per weight only when actually packed. If each group of 128 weights has one FP16 scale, metadata adds $2/128=0.015625$ bytes per weight. Total is 0.515625 bytes, excluding zero points, padding, and exceptions. A billion such weights take 515.625 MB rather than the 500 MB implied by the payload alone. Smaller groups can reduce numerical error while increasing metadata traffic and potentially reducing kernel efficiency.

Floating-point formats have different tradeoffs. Exponent bits determine dynamic range, mantissa bits determine local precision, and scaling granularity changes effective coverage. Avoid treating FP8, INT8, and four-bit formats as interchangeable labels. Record exact format, rounding, accumulation type, scale dtype, scale grouping, saturation handling, and whether activations, weights, or KV are quantized. A weight-only kernel still moves full-precision activations; a compressed KV cache affects attention rather than all model operations.

## Validate behavior on held-out tasks

Quality evaluation has several layers. First compare reconstructed tensors and linear outputs using absolute/relative error, outlier percentiles, and nonfinite counts. Then compare logits on identical prefixes with KL divergence, top-token agreement, and margins. Finally evaluate task success on held-out prompts representing the deployment: code, mathematical reasoning, long-context retrieval, structured output, or vision as appropriate. Mean perplexity alone can hide rare but consequential regressions. Keep calibration and evaluation examples disjoint, and freeze acceptance criteria before tuning.

Consider a task set with 1000 examples. The reference solves 820 and the quantized model solves 810. A one-point aggregate difference does not reveal whether the models disagree on the same cases, nor whether uncertainty excludes a practically meaningful loss. Save paired per-example outcomes. If the quantized version loses 25 reference successes but gains 15 failures, the net loss is ten; use a paired analysis or bootstrap over examples to quantify it. Independent repeated generations require a clearly defined sampling protocol. Do not tune on this held-out set after seeing the result.

## Distinguish compression from accelerated execution

Performance evaluation must separate a storage demonstration from accelerated execution. The supplied CPU lab quantizes and reconstructs values to expose numerical effects; it does not implement a production low-bit GEMM. For the accelerator extension, compare against a strong full-precision baseline on identical shapes, warmup policy, batch sizes, and outputs. Measure latency, throughput, peak memory, actual kernel choice, and scale/dequantization overhead. If compressed weights are expanded back to BF16 before every multiplication, any bandwidth benefit may vanish.

Quantized KV deserves a separate experiment from quantized weights. Its error is reused by future queries and may behave differently as context length grows. Sweep context length and attention patterns, including retrieval of an early fact after a long distractor span. Record scales and saturation per cache block. A short-prompt evaluation that passes does not establish long-context quality, and a weight-only accuracy report says nothing by itself about a compressed attention cache.

## Choose a measured quality–cost frontier

Finish with a Pareto frontier rather than a single winning bit width. Each point should specify accuracy uncertainty, SLO goodput, memory, and cost. Include an out-of-calibration stress set and one workload where a higher-precision configuration wins. The professional skill is choosing the least expensive representation that meets a measured quality contract, while being able to explain exactly where and why it fails.

exercises.prompt: A 4-bit scheme uses groups of 64 weights, each with a 2-byte scale and 2-byte zero-point. What are effective bits per weight?
exercises.hint: Convert metadata bytes per group into bits per weight.
exercises.solution: Payload is 4 bits/weight. Metadata is 4×8/64=0.5 bits/weight. Total is 4.5 bits/weight, or 0.5625 bytes, before padding and exceptional values.

exercises.title: Find the decision boundary
exercises.prompt: Two reference logits are 4.01 and 4.00. Quantization shifts them by −0.02 and +0.01. Compute the new greedy decision and explain why small average error can miss it.
exercises.hint: Compare the margin with the difference of perturbations.
exercises.solution: New logits are 3.99 and 4.01, so the second token wins. Original margin was 0.01 but relative perturbation was −0.03. A small mean error says little about near-tied decisions; inspect margin-conditioned disagreement and downstream task behavior.

exercises.title: Separate calibration from evaluation
exercises.prompt: You have 10000 prompts from deployment logs. Design a defensible calibration and test split for long-context and multilingual traffic.
exercises.hint: Stratify before tuning, and keep related sessions together.
exercises.solution: Reserve an untouched session-level test split stratified by language and length; create calibration and development partitions from the rest. Fit scales only on calibration data, choose settings on development, then evaluate once on test with per-slice and paired outcome uncertainty. Keep a distinct distribution-shift set and report it separately.

quiz.question: What breaks the s/2 reconstruction-error bound?
quiz.explanation: The s/2 bound is a nearest-rounding bound for values inside the representable range. Clipping an outlier to the largest representable value can create arbitrarily larger error relative to that rounding step.

quiz.question: Why is activation-aware evaluation useful?
options: Weight error is multiplied by the actual input vector
quiz.explanation: For a linear layer, output error is ΔW x. Errors on frequently large or consequential activation channels can matter much more than equally sized errors on inactive channels, so weight error alone is incomplete.

quiz.question: What proves an INT4 representation accelerates inference?
options: A quantization paper reports a speedup
Measured end-to-end speed with the actual packed kernel
quiz.explanation: A smaller checkpoint does not establish faster execution. Measure the actual packed kernel and the full inference path, including scale loads, unpacking, dequantization, and any change in achievable batch size.

quiz.question: Which identity supports equivalent channel rescaling before quantization?
quiz.explanation: For an invertible diagonal D, the factors D and D⁻¹ cancel in exact arithmetic. The transform preserves the original linear function before quantization while changing how rounding error is distributed afterward.

quiz.question: What should be fixed before tuning a quantizer?
options: Quality thresholds and a held-out evaluation protocol
quiz.explanation: Choose the quality contract and hold out evaluation data before fitting or selecting the quantizer. Repeatedly tuning against the test set can make reported accuracy reflect selection bias instead of generalization.

title: The cache is part of the architecture
subtitle: Derive state from the model instead of assuming every layer is a transformer.
outcomes: Derive cache storage for GQA, latent attention, windows, and recurrent state.
Separate exact algebraic changes from approximate sparsification.
Design cache rollback and prefix reuse for heterogeneous layers.
body:
An inference engine often begins with one mental picture: each layer appends a key and value for every token. That picture is convenient and increasingly incomplete. A model may compress keys and values into a shared latent vector, attend to a selected subset of positions, retain only a sliding suffix, or maintain a recurrent state with fixed size. These are different computational contracts. The right engine starts with a per-layer state inventory and derives memory, updates, reuse, and rollback from that inventory.

## Derive latent attention by moving linear maps

[DeepSeek-V2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04434) is a concrete introduction to multi-head latent attention, or MLA. To understand the idea, temporarily ignore positional terms. Suppose a token produces latent state $c_t\in\mathbb{R}^r$, and head $h$ reconstructs $k_t^h=W_K^hc_t$ and $v_t^h=W_V^hc_t$. A query's score satisfies

$$(q^h)^T k_t^h=(q^h)^TW_K^hc_t=((W_K^h)^Tq^h)^Tc_t.$$

Instead of materializing every full key, transform the query and compare it with the cached latent. For the output,

$$\sum_t a_t^h v_t^h=W_V^h\left(\sum_t a_t^h c_t\right).$$

The linear reconstruction can move outside the sum. This is an algebraic explanation of potential reuse, not the full DeepSeek implementation. Positional components need separate treatment, and learned projections and dimensions are architecture specific. Implement the simplified identities numerically before studying how actual positional information changes the cache.

## Compare state bytes before latency

Compare storage with a deliberately hypothetical configuration. GQA with 32 layers, eight KV heads, head width 128, and BF16 stores $2\times32\times8\times128\times2=131072$ bytes per token. A latent design storing 512 latent elements plus 64 positional elements per layer stores $32\times(512+64)\times2=36864$ bytes per token. The ratio is about 3.56. At 8192 positions those totals are 1 GiB and 288 MiB. These are teaching dimensions, not a claim about a named checkpoint. The latter calculation assumes one shared positional component of the stated width per layer; verify actual shapes before applying it.

Less storage does not automatically imply proportionally less latency. Transformed queries can be wider than original heads, and reconstruction may move compute into another stage. Cache layout, split reductions, low-precision representation, and batch occupancy determine the actual kernel. [FlashMLA](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/FlashMLA) is the implementation resource: inspect its supported modes and hardware for your pinned version rather than transferring one benchmark to every attention configuration.

## Account for the cost of selecting sparse positions

Sparse attention changes a different axis: which positions are read. If each query attends to $k$ of $s$ historical positions, its main attention work can shrink toward $O(kd)$ rather than $O(sd)$. But selecting those $k$ positions may itself require a scan, index lookup, or learned routing computation. Irregular gathers can waste bandwidth. Report selector time, attention time, and end-to-end time separately. A mask required by the trained architecture is part of the model; dropping extra positions from a dense model is an approximation and needs quality evaluation.

## Preserve windows through speculative rollback

Sliding windows have a useful bounded-state property. A window of 256 positions does not need to retain 8192 old positions for that layer's local attention. Yet a model containing both windowed and global layers still has a global cache component. Moreover, speculative decoding requires the ability to restore the window after rejected tokens. If a ring buffer overwrites old entries while draft tokens are uncommitted, rolling back only the write pointer cannot recover destroyed values. Keep a bounded undo area or delay destructive overwrites until commitment.

## Version every component of hybrid state

Recurrent layers introduce another state shape. A simplified update $s_t=As_{t-1}+Bx_t$ keeps state size independent of sequence length, but a prefix branch needs the state at the branch point. [Mamba](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752) provides a real selective-state architecture to examine beyond this toy recurrence. You cannot assume a conventional KV page table represents every layer correctly. Checkpointing recurrent states trades memory against replay work, and speculative rollback must restore a complete consistent version.

Consider prefix sharing in a hybrid model. Two requests sharing 4000 tokens can reuse global-attention pages, a final recurrent state at position 4000, and the last window suffix. Reusing only the global pages produces an inconsistent execution state even if those pages are correct. Cache identity must include model weights, adapter, positional scheme, precision, token prefix, and any modality preprocessing that changes model inputs. A shared prefix is a semantic object before it is a hash-table entry.

Memory reclamation also changes with state type. Immutable attention prefix pages can be reference counted, while a recurrent state updated in place must be copied before requests diverge. Give each request a logical state version and make sharing explicit. A useful adversarial test forks two requests at one prefix, advances only one, then verifies that the untouched request's next output is unchanged. This catches aliasing bugs that ordinary single-request numerical comparisons cannot expose.

## Build an architecture-aware experiment

The CPU cost-model lab is your starting point. Extend it with a list of layer types and explicit retained-state formulas. Then write a tiny algebra check for the absorbed latent equations and a ring-buffer rollback test that crosses its wrap boundary. Plot bytes per request against context length: global layers grow linearly, window layers plateau, and fixed-state layers stay flat. The sum reveals the real service limit. For hardware follow-up, profile only a supported implementation and clearly distinguish reduced state, reduced traffic, and measured latency. The durable skill is deriving engine invariants from architecture instead of forcing every model into yesterday's cache abstraction.

exercises.title: Inventory a hybrid cache
exercises.prompt: A model has 8 global layers and 24 window layers, each storing 4096 bytes per retained token. Context is 4096 tokens, window is 256. Ignore other state. Compute cache memory.
exercises.hint: Count retained token-layer pairs first.
exercises.solution: Global state: 8×4096×4096=134,217,728 bytes=128 MiB. Window state:24×256×4096=25,165,824 bytes=24 MiB. Total=152 MiB. Treating all 32 layers as global would predict 512 MiB.

exercises.title: Prove the absorbed value path
exercises.prompt: Given a_t scalar, c_t vectors, and fixed matrix W, show why sum_t a_t Wc_t = W sum_t a_t c_t, and identify a transformation that would invalidate moving it outside.
exercises.hint: Use linearity; nonlinear operations do not generally commute with the sum.
exercises.solution: Matrix multiplication distributes across addition and scalar multiplication. A nonlinear map such as ReLU(Wc_t) cannot generally move outside: sum a_t ReLU(Wc_t) differs from ReLU(W sum a_t c_t). Token-dependent W_t also prevents using one common outside matrix.

exercises.title: Catch destructive rollback
exercises.prompt: A window buffer holds positions 0–3. Draft positions 4–5 overwrite slots 0–1, then both are rejected. Why is resetting the pointer insufficient?
exercises.hint: The pointer records location, not the overwritten content.
exercises.solution: Positions 0–1 were destroyed but may be needed by the restored window. Save overwritten entries in an undo buffer, use copy-on-write pages, or stage draft values separately until acceptance. Test exact state restoration across the wrap boundary and multiple rejection lengths.

quiz.question: Which property justifies moving a shared value projection outside weighted summation?
quiz.explanation: A fixed linear matrix distributes over addition and scalar weighting, allowing W to move outside the sum. A token-dependent matrix or a nonlinear operation generally would not obey the same identity.

quiz.question: Why can a sparse attention kernel fail to reduce end-to-end latency?
options: Sparse attention always reads every token
Selection and irregular gathers can dominate
quiz.explanation: Selecting positions, loading indices, and gathering irregular memory can outweigh the attention work removed. Measure selector time and the full request, not only the sparse attention kernel in isolation.

quiz.question: What must a hybrid prefix cache preserve?
options: All architecture-specific state at the same prefix boundary
quiz.explanation: Every reused state component must describe the same prefix boundary. Global KV, a window suffix, and recurrent state can each be individually valid yet produce a wrong continuation when their versions disagree.

quiz.question: Which claim requires a quality study?
options: Dropping extra keys from an otherwise dense model
Moving a fixed linear projection algebraically
quiz.explanation: Extra key dropping changes which evidence contributes to the output of a dense model. It therefore needs task-quality evaluation, unlike an algebraically equivalent layout or correctly replicated immutable state.

quiz.question: What happens to window-layer storage after context exceeds the window?
options: It can plateau, excluding rollback and metadata overhead
quiz.explanation: A windowed layer only retains its bounded suffix once the context is longer than the window. Memory can therefore plateau, but rollback buffers, metadata, and any global layers still contribute to total state.

title: Read DeepInfer like a systems researcher
subtitle: Turn a production-derived release into falsifiable local experiments.
outcomes: Map a pinned release to explicit supported and missing components.
Trace an optimization from example to policy, invariant, and test.
Reproduce a mechanism without overstating hardware or production equivalence.
body:
A large open-source release can create the illusion that understanding its configuration flags means understanding the system. Reverse that relationship. Choose a performance claim, identify the mechanism that could make it true, trace the state and numerical invariants, then construct the smallest experiment capable of disproving your interpretation. DeepInfer is an advanced case study because kernels, expert placement, scheduling, model architecture, and reproducibility interact in one repository.

## Freeze the release and its scope

This lesson pins source inspected on October 21, 2026 to commit `9bd9cf243fc53ef9afbf8f04d391d989117d6ab9`. The [README](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/9bd9cf243fc53ef9afbf8f04d391d989117d6ab9/README.md) identifies offline inference for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs. It includes optimized kernels, expert balancing, speculative features, asynchronous scheduling, and specified reproducibility modes. It explicitly excludes the complete service KV system, vision/prefill/decode disaggregation deployment, and balancing across serving replicas. Source-level support for engine phases is not the same as a turnkey production service. These release facts have high confidence for the pinned snapshot; later versions require a fresh audit.

## Follow the runnable path and its guards

Start with a runnable path on paper. In [examples/offline_inference.py](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/9bd9cf243fc53ef9afbf8f04d391d989117d6ab9/examples/offline_inference.py), follow argument parsing, parallel-size relationships, common environment setup, engine construction, prompt preparation, generation, and output validation. Record shapes and ownership at each boundary. The example checks output structure and finite log probabilities and reports draft acceptance statistics. Those checks are useful evidence of intended behavior, but they do not establish production reliability or reproduce the throughput plots. Write a call graph with links to symbols, not a list of imported modules.

Next inspect [csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/9bd9cf243fc53ef9afbf8f04d391d989117d6ab9/csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp). Its engine-type distinction and constructor checks expose operational assumptions. For example, the completion-only engine rejects a configuration that would require recomputing preempted work through a nonexistent prefill channel. Translate this into a state-machine invariant: every recovery transition needs an execution path capable of rebuilding the state it discards. Find admission, abort, and cache-related transitions; for each, identify which component owns the sequence afterward. A useful code-reading note predicts a concrete failure if one guard were removed.

## Reproduce the expert-placement objective

Choose expert placement as your first bounded reproduction. [deepinfer/model_executor/eplb/policy.py](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/9bd9cf243fc53ef9afbf8f04d391d989117d6ab9/deepinfer/model_executor/eplb/policy.py) distinguishes logical experts from physical copies, assigns redundant copies, and places them using historical per-step load. The greedy placement evaluates an objective based on sums of per-step rank maxima. This is more informative than equalizing each expert's total historical tokens because correlations between experts matter. The returned maps are part of correctness: changing placement must not change which logical function a token receives.

A tiny counterexample explains the objective. Four experts have loads across two steps: $A=(10,0)$, $B=(10,0)$, $C=(0,10)$, and $D=(0,10)$. Every expert has total load ten. With two experts per rank, placement $(A,B)$ and $(C,D)$ produces rank loads $(20,0)$ then $(0,20)$, so the sum of step maxima is 40. Placement $(A,C)$ and $(B,D)$ produces $(10,10)$ at both steps, so the objective is 20. Aggregate totals cannot distinguish these layouts, but their synchronized critical paths differ by a factor of two in this linear toy model.

Reimplement that objective in a few lines, enumerate all legal placements for the tiny case, and compare a greedy policy with the exhaustive optimum. Then add noisy measurements and a phase change. This separates three claims: the mathematical objective captures an intended bottleneck, the algorithm approximately optimizes it, and optimizing it improves real accelerator latency. Only the first two are accessible through the CPU teaching experiment. A real GPU result needs dispatch, expert GEMMs, communication, and migration overhead measured on supported hardware.

## Separate implementation from deployment claims

Read the [deployment Q&A](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/blob/9bd9cf243fc53ef9afbf8f04d391d989117d6ab9/doc/inference_deployment_qa.md) as architecture context. It describes production choices and systems beyond the release. Maintain a three-column evidence ledger: repository implementation, author-reported deployment, and your independently measured result. Do not turn author-reported cluster numbers into results of your reproduction. If a detail appears only in prose, label it as a design description and identify the missing experiment or code needed to verify it.

## Bound the benefit of scheduler overlap

For a second study, examine CPU/device overlap with a critical-path model. If device work costs 8 ms and CPU scheduling 3 ms, serial execution costs 11 ms. Ideal overlap costs at least 8 ms, yielding an upper-bound speedup of 1.375 before coordination. A 2× observed improvement would need another explanation, such as changed batching, removed synchronization, or a different workload. This arithmetic makes you a better source reader: optimistic marketing language becomes a measurable claim about a timeline.

## Turn source reading into a regression argument

Treat tests as executable statements of intent. Locate the policy tests, identify which invariants they assert, and design one missing adversarial input rather than assuming coverage is complete. Empty history, equal loads, insufficient physical slots, and alternating hot experts probe different assumptions. A passing test suite increases confidence only in the properties actually checked. Record your additional case and the expected outcome so the source note becomes a reusable regression argument instead of a one-time reading summary.

Use the experiment template to capture commit, submodules, dependencies, model checkpoint, exact flags, hardware topology, and workload. Build nothing merely to prove enthusiasm; on unsupported hardware, finish the policy reproduction and source map. On supported hardware, begin with the repository's documented example and checks before altering a single mechanism. Your exit artifact is a technical note with a falsifiable hypothesis, a minimal reproducer, at least one counterexample, and a clear boundary between confirmed code behavior and untested production inference.

title: Pixels become queueing decisions
subtitle: Serve images by their computational shape and information value.
outcomes: Trace image bytes through preprocessing, encoding, and language decoding.
Estimate visual-token and cache cost before admission.
Measure a task-specific resolution–latency tradeoff with correct cache identity.
body:
A vision-language request begins before the language model sees a token. Image transfer, decompression, resize, crop generation, normalization, device transfer, visual encoding, projection, language prefill, and output generation can each dominate a different workload. Optimizing the decoder while ignoring an overloaded CPU image pipeline is a common failure. Draw the complete timeline first, and give every stage an input size, output size, queue, and measurement boundary.

## Count computational shapes, not images

The key conceptual move is to stop counting images and start counting computational shapes. A tiny image and a high-resolution document may both be one request but produce very different numbers of visual tokens. [Qwen2-VL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12191) is a useful dynamic-resolution example; [Qwen2.5-VL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923) adds another architecture to compare. The point is not that these are universally best models. Their explicit processing choices make the conversion from pixels into sequence work inspectable.

## Derive pixels, tokens, and prefill work

Use a simple hypothetical processor to make the conversion concrete. An image of width $W$ and height $H$, patch size $p$, and spatial merge factor $m$ per dimension produces approximately

$$N_v=\frac{\lceil W/p\rceil\lceil H/p\rceil}{m^2}$$

visual tokens, assuming compatible padding and no additional crops or special tokens. For a 448×448 image with $p=14$ and $m=2$, there are 1024 patches and 256 merged tokens. At 896×896, there are 4096 patches and 1024 merged tokens. Doubling each side quadruples the visual sequence. Real processors may resize to supported multiples, create tiles, or add temporal grouping; read the processor's returned grid and count actual embeddings rather than treating this approximation as a universal formula.

If the text prompt has 256 tokens, these examples produce language prefill lengths 512 and 1280 before special tokens. A dense attention score component scales roughly with sequence length squared, so its operation-count ratio is $(1280/512)^2=6.25$. MLP and projection terms grow linearly, and optimized kernels change runtime behavior, so the whole prefill is not automatically 6.25 times slower. Cache growth is linear in the inserted visual positions for ordinary causal self-attention. This one example shows why a pixel budget affects both latency and concurrency.

## Spend resolution on task-relevant evidence

Quality determines how far resolution can shrink. A scene-category question may need coarse layout; reading a serial number requires small glyphs to survive preprocessing. Build evaluation slices for small text, spatial relations, counting, fine-grained recognition, and document structure. Hold prompts and output budgets fixed while varying pixel/token limits. Record task scores per slice and confidence intervals, not merely whether the outputs look plausible. A low-resolution model that confidently invents digits has not satisfied an OCR task even if its average description sounds correct.

Dynamic policies can allocate pixels by task. A cheap first pass might identify a relevant region and a second pass inspect that crop at higher resolution. Account for both passes, routing errors, and added queueing. Compare against a fixed-budget baseline with the same average compute and against a strong full-resolution reference. If the first pass misses the relevant region, the second pass cannot recover information it never receives. This creates a measurable quality–latency frontier rather than a blanket claim that fewer visual tokens are better.

## Cache the exact visual computation

Feature caching can remove repeated encoder work, but its identity is richer than the image filename. Include image content, crop/resize policy, normalization, model and processor versions, adapter, precision, and any position-dependent representation. Cache raw encoder embeddings only when their contract allows reuse across prompts; multimodal decoder KV depends on surrounding sequence context and positions. Two identical image bytes inserted at different positions may share encoder work while requiring different language-model state. Validate reuse against uncached logits on a small deterministic case.

## Budget each stage of a multimodal batch

Batching must recognize modality heterogeneity. Grouping images by shape can reduce padding, but waiting too long to fill a shape bucket harms latency. Large visual requests can also monopolize language prefill. Introduce separate budgets for encoder pixels or patches, language tokens, and KV memory. Reserve capacity across stages so a finished encoder does not produce an unlimited queue of embeddings awaiting prefill. If you disaggregate the vision encoder, count embedding transport and serialization instead of assuming it is free.

## Measure the whole request

The measurement record should contain image bytes received, decoded dimensions, crop count, patch grid, actual visual-token count, preprocessing duration, encoder queue and execution time, prefill queue and execution time, output tokens, and user-visible completion time. Define TTFT from request arrival including image transport if that is what the application experiences; also report a server-received boundary if network conditions are variable. These two measurements answer different questions and should not be merged.

The supplied cost-model lab is a CPU baseline for sequence and memory accounting. This week's extension adds the hypothetical visual processor and stage costs; it does not run a pretrained VLM. For a GPU project, choose a supported checkpoint, pin its processor, and build a small held-out visual workload. Reproduce actual token counts before optimizing. Your final artifact should show which resolution policy meets a concrete task-quality target at the lowest SLO-qualified cost, plus at least one image category where reducing visual tokens fails.

exercises.title: Budget a visual prompt
exercises.prompt: For a hypothetical 672×448 image, p=14 and m=2, compute visual tokens. Add a 512-token text prompt and calculate cache bytes at 64 KiB per token.
exercises.hint: Both dimensions divide exactly; ignore special tokens as stated.
exercises.solution: Patches=(672/14)×(448/14)=48×32=1536. Merged visual tokens=1536/4=384. Total=896 tokens. Cache=896×65536=58,720,256 bytes=56 MiB, before output tokens and metadata.

exercises.title: Identify the bottleneck
exercises.prompt: A request takes 45 ms preprocessing, 20 ms encoding, 15 ms prefill, and 20 ms decode. You halve decode time. What is end-to-end speedup?
exercises.hint: Sum the complete timeline, assuming serial stages.
exercises.solution: Original=100 ms. New=45+20+15+10=90 ms. Speedup=100/90≈1.111. The decoder improved 2× but whole-request latency only 10%; preprocessing deserves investigation.

exercises.title: Design a reusable feature key
exercises.prompt: Two requests use the same JPEG but different crops and adapters. What should an encoder-feature cache key include?
exercises.hint: Cache identity must describe the actual computation.
exercises.solution: Include content digest, crop coordinates, resize/padding, normalization, processor version, encoder weights/version, adapter if it changes the encoder, and precision. If only the language adapter differs, encoder reuse may remain valid but decoder KV reuse still needs its own complete identity. Prove the intended boundary with uncached equivalence tests.

quiz.question: Doubling both dimensions of an image usually changes patch count by:
quiz.explanation: At fixed patch size and compatible dimensions, doubling width and height multiplies image area by four. Patch count follows area, before any model-specific resizing, tiling, merging, or token caps.

quiz.question: Why should image count not be the sole encoder batch budget?
options: Resolution and crop counts produce very different work
quiz.explanation: Images can differ greatly in dimensions, tiling, and crop count. Those choices determine patch work and memory, so a batch of ten small images need not cost as much as one large document.

quiz.question: What is required before reusing decoder KV for the same image?
options: Matching model/input/position context and cache semantics
quiz.explanation: Decoder KV depends on the complete model input, token positions, and model configuration. Identical image bytes may allow encoder-feature reuse while still producing different context-dependent decoder state.

quiz.question: Which quality slice is especially likely to fail after aggressive downsampling?
quiz.explanation: Aggressive downsampling can erase small glyphs before encoding, so the lost evidence is unavailable to the language model. Good broad-scene descriptions do not demonstrate preserved OCR performance.

quiz.question: A 6.25× dense attention operation increase implies what about total prefill latency?
options: No fixed total latency ratio without the other terms and measured kernels
quiz.explanation: The 6.25 ratio applies to the modeled dense attention component, not the entire prefill. Linear projections, MLP work, padding, and hardware utilization must be included before predicting total latency.
