title: A fast answer to an old frame is still old
subtitle: Design causal streams around age, deadlines, and evidence.
outcomes: Distinguish processing latency, observation age, and update cadence.
Compare FIFO, dropping, and latest-observation queues under overload.
Preserve arrival-time provenance and causal cache semantics.
body:
A video service can process every frame efficiently and still describe a scene that no longer exists. This happens when capture outpaces inference and an obedient FIFO queue preserves all the wrong work. Real-time perception needs an explicit contract about timeliness: how old may the evidence be when the answer is used, which brief events must be retained, and what should happen when the server cannot keep up? Raw frames per second cannot answer those questions.

## Define age separately from processing latency

Record at least four times for each observation: capture, arrival at the service, inference start, and result availability. Processing latency is result time minus inference start. End-to-end observation latency is result time minus capture. At wall time $t$, age of information is

$$A(t)=t-u(t),$$

where $u(t)$ is the capture timestamp of the freshest observation represented by the latest available result. The [Age of Information survey](https://www.mit.edu/~modiano/papers/CV_J_122preprint.pdf) develops this timeliness perspective. A result can have low processing latency but high age because it waited in transport or a queue. Between results, age grows even when no inference is running.

## Watch a FIFO queue fall behind

Work through a deterministic timeline. Frames arrive every 50 ms, while inference takes 200 ms. FIFO begins frame zero at 0 ms and returns it at 200 ms, then begins the frame captured at 50 ms and returns it at 400 ms. The second result is already 350 ms old. After $n$ completed frames, age at completion is $200n-50(n-1)=150n+50$ ms. The queue grows without bound because arrival rate is 20/s and service rate is 5/s.

Now keep only the latest waiting frame while allowing the active inference to finish. At 200 ms, choose the newest frame available, captured at 200 ms under a stated tie-ordering rule; it finishes at 400 ms with age 200 ms. At each completion, age remains near service time, and immediately before the next completion it can approach 400 ms. If capture is asynchronous, add up to one capture interval to these simple bounds. Report both age at result delivery and time-average or high-percentile age over the whole timeline; sampling only completions hides the stale intervals between them.

## Replace waiting work without starving active work

Do not confuse replacement of waiting work with preemption of active work. Cancelling a 200 ms inference every time a 50 ms frame arrives can prevent any result from completing. A practical default is one non-preemptive active item plus one replaceable pending item, with deadline checks before starting expensive work. True preemption is useful only if execution can resume or partial work has value and cancellation overhead is controlled. Measure the policy rather than assuming that maximum freshness means restarting constantly.

## Protect the events that dropping can erase

Dropping frames is not universally correct. A 100 ms event between sampled observations can disappear, and a latest-only service may never report it. Maintain a lightweight event path or a bounded history buffer when transient recall matters. One design uses cheap motion or detector updates at high frequency and slower semantic descriptions asynchronously. Late semantic results attach to their source interval and track IDs instead of overwriting the present state. Evaluate both freshness and event recall; improving one can damage the other.

## Preserve time and information provenance

Time provenance is especially important with multiple cameras. Capture clocks may disagree, arrivals may be reordered, and network jitter may differ by stream. Record clock domain, synchronization estimate, and uncertainty. Never subtract timestamps from unrelated monotonic clocks as though they shared an epoch. When combining observations, store their capture intervals separately. A sentence produced at 12:00:05 from frames captured at 12:00:01 is evidence about the earlier scene, even if its text is confident.

Causal evaluation must replay arrival order. If a model caches representations as observations arrive, later questions, future camera calibration, or future frame selection cannot retroactively change the earlier cached computation unless the system explicitly recomputes it and charges that cost. Freeze the metadata available at each arrival. Compare a live causal mode against any offline oracle as separate experiments. A retrospective video benchmark can be useful, but it does not establish streaming behavior merely because outputs are emitted one at a time.

## Evaluate timely recall as well as freshness

For an illustrative optimization objective, define timely recall as the fraction of ground-truth events correctly reported before their deadline. A system detecting 90 of 100 events but only 40 before deadline has timely recall 40%, while a system detecting 80 with 70 on time has 70%. Neither number should replace ordinary recall; show both to reveal the tradeoff. Also measure stale-result overwrites, duplicate reports, per-camera starvation, and how latency changes during bursts.

The supplied freshness lab is a CPU event simulation, not a live camera or VLM. Run FIFO and latest-observation policies at identical capture and service rates, then vary service-time jitter, transport delays, and short-event durations. Extend it with a separate event-recall calculation and a two-camera fairness rule. For a real service, preserve frame IDs through every stage and log sampled timestamps at output commitment. The final demonstration should make queue age visible, show exactly which frames were skipped, and explain why the chosen policy meets the application's evidence and freshness contract.

exercises.title: Trace a stale FIFO
exercises.prompt: Frames arrive at 0,40,80,... ms; service takes 120 ms. What are the completion time and age for the fourth FIFO frame?
exercises.hint: The fourth frame is indexed three and was captured at 120 ms.
exercises.solution: It completes at 4×120=480 ms, giving age 480−120=360 ms. Processing itself took 120 ms; queueing caused the other 240 ms.

exercises.title: Measure time-average age
exercises.prompt: A latest-only system delivers results every 200 ms, each based on an observation 200 ms old. Assuming linear growth between deliveries and no jitter, compute average and peak age.
exercises.hint: Each interval is a sawtooth from 200 to 400 ms.
exercises.solution: Average age is (200+400)/2=300 ms. Peak approaches 400 ms just before the next delivery. Reporting only the delivery age of 200 ms understates continuous staleness.

exercises.title: Detect future-information leakage
exercises.prompt: A replay uses camera poses estimated from the full video to encode every earlier frame, while claiming an online unknown-camera system. Design a valid comparison.
exercises.hint: The information set at encoding time must match deployment.
exercises.solution: Create causal replay that supplies only poses available by each frame arrival, preserving uncertainty and charging any later recomputation. Compare separately with an offline full-video-pose oracle. If future poses alter earlier cached keys without recomputation, the streaming claim is invalid.

quiz.question: A frame waits 600 ms then takes 50 ms to process. Its age at delivery is at least:
quiz.explanation: Age includes the 600 ms queue wait and the 50 ms processing interval, totaling at least 650 ms. Any earlier capture or transport delay makes the evidence older still.

quiz.question: Which policy can starve all completions when arrivals are faster than service?
options: Restart active inference on every new frame
Finish active work then choose newest
quiz.explanation: If each arrival restarts work before its service time elapses, no inference may ever finish. Replacing only waiting work permits the active item to complete and avoids this form of starvation.

quiz.question: Why can latest-only scheduling reduce event recall?
options: Short events may occur only in skipped frames
quiz.explanation: A brief event may exist only in frames that the latest-only policy skips. Fresh results and complete temporal coverage are distinct goals, so event recall must be evaluated alongside age.

quiz.question: Which timestamp defines the evidence age of a result?
options: Capture time of the observation it actually used
Current time inserted into the prompt
quiz.explanation: The capture timestamp locates the evidence in the world timeline. Rendering a result later or inserting the current time into its text does not make the underlying observation more recent.

quiz.question: What is required for a causal streaming benchmark?
options: All metadata from the complete recording
Replay using only information available at each arrival
The word streaming in the API
quiz.explanation: At each replay step, the model may use only information available by that arrival. Future poses, frames, or questions cannot silently modify earlier cached computation; explicit recomputation must be accounted for.

title: The action has a deadline
subtitle: Treat inference as part of a closed-loop system, not a token stream.
outcomes: Budget observation-to-action latency at a fixed control rate.
Design asynchronous chunk execution with explicit temporal alignment.
Evaluate deadline misses, discontinuities, and closed-loop task outcomes.
body:
An action prediction is useful only at the time and state for which it was intended. A robot does not pause its dynamics while a large model finishes thinking. The central systems problem is therefore temporal alignment: which observation generated the action, how much time passed, which actions have already executed, and when the new prediction should take over. A high action-generation rate can coexist with poor control if the generated actions are stale or discontinuous.

## Separate the policy loop from the control loop

Separate the control loop from the policy inference loop. A low-level controller might consume actions every $\Delta=20$ ms, or 50 Hz, while a learned policy takes 180 ms to produce a chunk of 25 actions. The chunk covers 500 ms of nominal control time, but inference latency spans nine control ticks. Running inference synchronously and waiting at every chunk boundary creates a 180 ms gap unless another controller supplies behavior. A chunk gives scheduling room; it does not erase the delay between sensing and acting.

## Budget observation-to-action delay

Write a full observation-to-action budget:

$$T_{oa}=T_{capture}+T_{transport}+T_{queue}+T_{preprocess}+T_{policy}+T_{return}+T_{dispatch}.$$

Choose boundaries carefully: capture can mean exposure midpoint or completed frame acquisition, and actuator dispatch can mean command submission or actual controller application. Document the convention. For an illustrative pipeline with 15 ms capture/transport, 20 ms queue/preprocessing, 120 ms policy, and 25 ms return/dispatch, total latency is 180 ms. Reporting only the 120 ms policy duration understates the feedback delay by one third.

## Reserve enough future actions

Asynchronous execution begins a new inference before the current action buffer runs out. If measured p99 inference-to-delivery latency is 180 ms and control period is 20 ms, at least nine future ticks are needed just to cover that quantile. Reserving eleven ticks adds 40 ms of timing margin. That is a scheduling calculation, not a proof of control stability. Long open-loop intervals can be harmful when contacts, moving targets, or disturbances change the state rapidly. Measure the task's sensitivity to delay rather than choosing horizon solely to eliminate buffer underflow.

## Align chunks while the world moves

Temporal alignment becomes difficult when a new chunk arrives. Suppose a chunk was predicted from observation time $t_0$ and delivered at $t_0+180$ ms. If its first action was intended for $t_0$, playing it now shifts the entire plan nine ticks late. One possible policy discards expired elements and starts at the matching time index, but this assumes the remaining prediction is valid given what actually happened. Another predicts while conditioning on actions that are already committed. [Real-Time Execution of Action Chunking Flow Policies](https://www.pi.website/download/real_time_chunking.pdf) studies asynchronous chunk generation with committed-prefix constraints. Read its algorithm before treating arbitrary chunk concatenation as equivalent.

Model families change the runtime. Autoregressive action tokens require sequential decoding and a conversion to physical commands. Diffusion or flow policies iterate through denoising/integration steps over a chunk. Reducing those steps can lower latency while changing action quality, just as reducing image resolution changes visual evidence. Batch several independent robots only if the resulting waiting time meets each robot's deadline; throughput maximization across robots is not automatically compatible with a tight control period.

## Make the action contract explicit

The [openpi remote-inference documentation](https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi/blob/main/docs/remote_inference.md) provides a concrete client/server boundary and returns action arrays with a horizon dimension. Study the observation transformation, image resize, normalization, and action convention together. Units, coordinate frames, joint ordering, and absolute-versus-delta semantics are part of correctness. A faster network path cannot repair a degrees-versus-radians error. Pin both client and server versions so a preprocessing change does not silently alter policy inputs.

Implement an action envelope around every result: observation ID, capture timestamp, policy version, chunk start time, action period, coordinate frame, and validity interval. The consumer checks that envelope before admitting a chunk. Use a monotonic sequence number to reject out-of-order responses. Do not let a late older request replace a newer plan merely because it arrived last. Define behavior when no valid action remains using the controller's supported fallback; evaluate that behavior in simulation before physical integration.

## Evaluate the closed loop

Measure the closed loop, not just the server. Log observation age at each applied action, buffer underflows, deadline-miss rate, chunk-boundary discontinuity, completion time, and task success. For a position-command sequence, a simple diagnostic is $\|a_t-a_{t-1}\|$ at handoffs compared with within-chunk values. It is not a universal smoothness metric: velocity, acceleration, and task-specific constraints may matter more. Aggregate averages can hide a few catastrophic pauses, so inspect the entire timing trace and worst supported conditions.

The supplied freshness simulator is a safe CPU starting point for scheduling concepts; it is not a pretrained VLA or a physical control loop. Extend it with a fixed-rate action consumer, finite action chunks, variable inference delay, and an explicit fallback event. Compare blocking, naive asynchronous splicing, and temporally aligned replacement. Then evaluate on a recorded or simulated closed-loop task with disturbances. Replaying observations alone can test timing but cannot establish closed-loop task success because actions no longer influence future observations. Your final report must state this boundary clearly and demonstrate both a deadline failure and a recovered operating region.

exercises.title: Reserve enough action ticks
exercises.prompt: A 25 Hz controller receives policy chunks with p99 delivery latency 260 ms. How many ticks cover that delay, and how many cover it with two ticks of extra margin?
exercises.hint: The control period is 40 ms; round upward.
exercises.solution: ceil(260/40)=7 ticks cover 280 ms. Adding two ticks gives 9 ticks, covering 360 ms. This budgets scheduling slack but does not prove the policy remains accurate for that open-loop duration.

exercises.title: Align a delayed chunk
exercises.prompt: A 20-step chunk with 20 ms spacing is timestamped to begin at 1000 ms and arrives at 1120 ms. Under a strict time-index interpretation, which index is current and how many elements remain including it?
exercises.hint: Index zero corresponds to 1000 ms.
exercises.solution: Elapsed=120 ms=6 ticks, so index 6 is current and 20−6=14 elements remain. This arithmetic alone does not justify execution: check actual executed actions and state compatibility before using the suffix.

exercises.title: Separate replay from closed-loop evidence
exercises.prompt: A recorded-observation replay shows zero missed deadlines under a new scheduler. Can you claim robot success improved? Design the missing experiment.
exercises.hint: In replay, actions cannot change subsequent observations.
exercises.solution: No. Replay establishes timing behavior on that fixed trace. Run matched simulated episodes with actions feeding the environment, held-out initial states and disturbances, identical policy weights, and repeated seeds. Report success, completion time, action age, and failures. Use paired episodes when appropriate.

quiz.question: A 50 Hz control loop and 160 ms policy latency imply a delay of:
quiz.explanation: A 50 Hz loop has a period of 1000/50 = 20 ms. A 160 ms inference spans eight control ticks, which must be covered by valid actions or an explicitly defined fallback.

quiz.question: What must happen when an older response arrives after a newer plan?
options: Reject it or reconcile explicitly using timestamps and generation IDs
Append it at the end blindly
quiz.explanation: A later arrival may have been computed from an older observation and correspond to expired action times. Sequence IDs and timestamps let the consumer reject or explicitly reconcile it instead of overwriting a newer plan.

quiz.question: Which evidence establishes closed-loop task performance?
options: Episodes where applied actions influence future observations
quiz.explanation: Closed-loop evaluation requires applied actions to influence the environment and therefore the next observations. Recorded-observation replay can establish timing behavior but cannot demonstrate resulting task success.

quiz.question: Why is action chunking not a complete latency solution?
options: Actions can be based on old observations or misaligned at handoffs
quiz.explanation: An action horizon provides scheduling slack but does not guarantee that its actions remain valid as the world changes. Delayed or incompatible chunks can still create stale feedback and discontinuous handoffs.

quiz.question: Which optimization requires action-quality validation?
quiz.explanation: Reducing denoising or flow-solver steps changes the approximation used to generate the action chunk. The latency reduction must therefore be evaluated together with action quality and closed-loop task outcomes.

title: Make the result survive another machine
subtitle: A benchmark is an argument with executable evidence.
outcomes: Write a falsifiable hypothesis and identify confounders.
Measure throughput and tail latency without changing offered load.
Package repeated-run evidence with uncertainty and an honest scope.
body:
A speedup is a ratio, and almost every term in that ratio can be accidentally changed. The model revision, tokenizer, prompt mix, output length, cache state, power limit, compiler, precision, batching, and measurement boundary can all move the result. Systems research begins by making the comparison interpretable. Your goal this week is an experiment that another engineer can rerun, criticize, and extend without asking what the numbers meant.

## State the claim and its success contract

Write the claim before the code. For example: “At fixed hardware and quality, our policy increases requests completed within TTFT ≤ 1 s and p95 per-request inter-token gap ≤ 80 ms on held-out bursty traces.” Define whether every token gap or a per-request statistic enters eligibility. Define how cancelled, rejected, and timed-out requests count. These choices are part of the objective; changing them after seeing results is changing the question.

Use an explicit goodput estimator:

$$G=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[\text{request }i\text{ meets the declared contract}]}{T_{measurement}}.$$

## Keep offered load independent of server speed

Keep the offered trace fixed across variants. In an open-loop load generator, request arrivals follow the trace independently of responses. In a closed-loop generator, a client often waits for a response before sending its next request, so a slower server receives fewer arrivals. That can conceal overload and distort latency comparisons. Closed-loop testing is valid for workloads that actually behave that way, but it answers a different question. Record scheduled arrival time and actual send time to detect generator bottlenecks.

A simple example shows the danger. Variant A takes one second per request and variant B takes two. Ten closed-loop clients offer roughly ten requests/s to A but only five to B at saturation. Comparing their latency distributions as if both saw ten requests/s is false. An open-loop trace at ten requests/s exposes B's backlog. If the generator itself cannot send on time, measure delay from scheduled arrival or explicitly report the missed arrivals instead of silently resetting the clock when the send finally occurs.

## Separate warmup, execution, and instrumentation

Separate cold start, warm steady state, and cache-assisted service. Compilation, model loading, graph capture, allocator growth, and network setup belong to cold-start measurements when deployment requires them. They should not be mixed into a steady-state kernel median by accident. Conversely, an always-warm microbenchmark does not establish autoscaling recovery time. The [PyTorch benchmark recipe](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/benchmark) explains warmup-aware repeated timing; use runtime-aware timers and verify synchronization for your measurement scope.

For GPU microbenchmarks, ensure work completion is included. For end-to-end throughput, avoid placing a device synchronization after every operator because that destroys the overlap you intend to measure. Profile a diagnostic run separately from the timing run and quantify instrumentation overhead. Record device model, memory, topology, driver/runtime, compiler, power settings, and software commits. The [PyTorch reproducibility notes](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.14/notes/randomness.html) distinguish seeding from stronger reproducibility guarantees; state the actual numerical contract instead of promising cross-platform bitwise identity.

## Match uncertainty to independent evidence

Repeat independent runs and preserve per-request records. A million correlated requests from one run are not a million independent experiments. Cache warmup, thermal drift, workload phases, and shared failures create dependence. Alternate or randomize variant order; pair runs on the same trace; summarize run-level differences. If you bootstrap, resample independent runs or defensible workload blocks rather than pretending every adjacent token latency is independent. Show the interval and method, not only a mean speedup.

Tail estimates need enough evidence. With 100 observations, p99 is determined by approximately the largest one or two values depending on the quantile convention. That is unstable evidence for a rare-tail claim. If zero failures occur in 100 independent trials, the approximate 95% upper bound from the rule of three is 3%, not zero. More generally, the exact one-sided zero-failure bound solves $(1-p)^n=0.05$, giving $p=1-0.05^{1/n}$. Report sample counts and independence assumptions alongside tail metrics.

## Use ablations and honest aggregation

Use ablations to connect the improvement to a mechanism. Compare baseline, feature A, feature B, and A+B under the same workload and tuning budget. If A+B improves but neither alone does, investigate interaction rather than attributing the whole gain to the feature you prefer. Also vary the parameter that should control the effect: cache reuse for prefix caching, acceptance for speculation, skew for expert placement, or service delay for freshness scheduling. A predicted trend that fails is valuable evidence against your explanation.

Aggregate speedups carefully. If a baseline takes 1 ms on one shape and 100 ms on another, while a variant takes 0.5 ms and 110 ms, its per-shape speedups are 2 and about 0.91. Yet processing one of each takes 110.5 ms instead of 101 ms, so the workload slows down. An unweighted average of ratios answers a different question from total workload time. Publish the workload weights and report both per-shape results and the aggregate metric that matches deployment.

## Package the evidence for another engineer

The [OSDI artifact guidance](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi24/call-for-artifacts) is a useful standard for making evidence inspectable. Package commands, environment details, raw data, correctness checks, plotting code, and expected qualitative results. Include a low-cost smoke test and a full-run budget. Use the course experiment template for one earlier lab and reproduce a result from a clean directory. The week's deliverable is not a flattering chart: it is a defensible claim with a baseline, uncertainty, a counterexample, and enough executable detail that someone else can discover your mistake if you made one.

exercises.title: Compute a failure bound
exercises.prompt: You observe zero failures in 200 independent trials. Give the rule-of-three estimate and exact one-sided 95% upper bound.
exercises.solution: Rule of three gives 3/200=1.5%. Exact bound is 1−0.05^(1/200)≈1.487%. Zero observed failures does not prove zero risk; dependence between trials would weaken this calculation.

exercises.title: Unmask a throughput comparison
exercises.prompt: A baseline has 1000 offered requests and 700 SLO successes in 100 s. A variant has 600 offered and 540 successes in 100 s. Which has higher measured goodput, and is the architectural comparison fair?
exercises.hint: Goodput uses qualifying completions; fairness also requires matched offered workload.
exercises.solution: Baseline goodput=7/s, variant=5.4/s. Variant has higher success fraction (90% vs 70%) but lower measured goodput. Because offered loads differ, this does not establish a fair capacity comparison; rerun the same trace and sweep matched offered rates.

exercises.title: Design a four-way ablation
exercises.prompt: An engine changes chunked prefill and prefix caching together and improves latency. Design the minimum factorial comparison.
exercises.hint: Use the two features as binary factors.
exercises.solution: Run neither, chunking only, caching only, and both, with identical model, resources, offered trace, cache initialization, and tuning budget. Repeat run order randomly. Measure mechanism-specific counters: prefill interruption/gaps and reused token counts, then test whether the combined effect is additive or interactive.

quiz.question: Why can closed-loop generation conceal overload?
options: Slow responses reduce subsequent offered arrivals
It is identical to open-loop replay
quiz.explanation: When clients wait for responses before sending more work, a slower server automatically receives fewer new requests. That feedback can hide the queue growth that a fixed external arrival process would produce.

quiz.question: Zero failures in 100 independent trials implies approximately what 95% upper bound?
quiz.explanation: The rule of three estimates a one-sided 95% upper failure-probability bound of 3/n. With n=100 independent trials it is about 3%, so zero observed failures does not establish a zero failure probability.

quiz.question: What is a strong unit for resampling repeated correlated workloads?
quiz.explanation: Adjacent requests can share cache state, thermal conditions, bursts, and failures. Resampling independent runs or justified blocks preserves more of that dependence than treating every token as an independent trial.

quiz.question: What should a profiling run establish before its timing is used?
options: Instrumentation overhead is understood and does not invalidate the comparison
More trace events always mean more speed
quiz.explanation: Profilers and forced synchronization can change execution order, overhead, and overlap. Establish their effect and use a separate timing run when needed so the measured system matches the claimed operating mode.

quiz.question: Which artifact best supports reproducibility?
options: Pinned code, raw data, commands, environment, correctness checks, and plots
A rounded speedup in a README
Only a container tag called latest
quiz.explanation: Reproducibility requires an executable chain from a pinned environment and inputs through correctness checks to raw measurements and figures. A screenshot or an unversioned latest tag cannot supply that chain.

title: Earn the right to make a new claim
subtitle: One narrow mechanism, one strong baseline, one result that survives scrutiny.
outcomes: Turn a bottleneck into a bounded original hypothesis.
Design a matched evaluation with ablations and failure regions.
Publish a reproducible research artifact with calibrated claims.
body:
Finishing a course does not place someone at the research frontier. Producing a result that changes what a competent engineer should do is a stronger test. Your capstone is therefore not “build a faster inference engine.” It is a narrow claim about a mechanism, workload, and constraint, supported by code and evidence. A negative result can pass if it explains a widely plausible idea's failure and rules out the obvious alternative explanations.

## Choose a bottleneck you can actually test

Begin with the bottleneck ledger you built throughout the course. Choose one observed limitation that is both consequential and experimentally accessible: expert placement chasing a changing distribution, speculation wasting work at high occupancy, visual-token budgets harming small-text quality, or stale observations dominating an otherwise fast VLA server. Avoid choosing a topic solely because its repository is new. You need a measurable causal story and enough resources to test it credibly.

Write a hypothesis with an intervention, mechanism, outcome, and boundary. For example: “A migration-budgeted expert placement policy improves p99 layer latency on phase-changing routing traces by avoiding replans whose predicted savings cannot repay movement cost.” The mechanism is a break-even rule; the outcome is measured latency; the boundary is a workload with changes on a comparable timescale. A static uniform trace should show little benefit, making it a useful control. CPU simulation can test the control logic, while a hardware latency claim requires actual movement and execution measurements.

## Select one capstone track

Three capstone tracks connect the course projects. The engine track studies one scheduler or cache policy in the small serving engine, with an established runtime as a reference where feasible. The distributed track studies dispatch, replication, or placement using the MoE lab and then a real multi-device implementation if available. The embodied track studies video/VLA freshness under strict deadlines, with a closed-loop simulator for action-performance claims. Choose one track deeply. Combining all three before proving any mechanism usually creates a large demo with an ambiguous conclusion.

## Predict a break-even boundary

Derive a prediction before running the main evaluation. Suppose your expert policy estimates migration cost $C_m$ and per-step saving $\Delta t$. It should migrate only if the useful horizon $H$ satisfies

$$H\Delta t>C_m+M,$$

where $M$ is a margin for estimation error. With $C_m=60$ ms, $\Delta t=0.3$ ms, and $M=15$ ms, break-even requires more than 250 useful steps. Test around that boundary: 50, 150, 250, 500, and 1000-step phases. If the policy claims benefits equally everywhere, either the model is wrong or another implementation difference is driving the result. Both possibilities are worth investigating.

## Set a fair baseline and correctness contract

Build a baseline ladder. Include the simplest reasonable policy, a well-tuned existing method, your proposal, and an oracle only when it clarifies the remaining opportunity. Give deployable variants equal resources and comparable tuning effort. The oracle can know future phase duration, but label that information advantage explicitly. Freeze training/calibration traces separately from evaluation traces. A controller tuned on the exact test phase sequence may simply memorize it, which is not workload adaptation.

Define correctness at the lowest relevant level and quality at the highest. A placement optimization preserves logical expert outputs; a speculative optimization preserves the stated sampling contract; a visual-token policy may intentionally approximate and must meet a held-out quality threshold; a VLA scheduler must preserve action units and timestamps while proving task success in a closed loop. “It ran without crashing” is an execution result, not a correctness or quality result.

## Map the operating and failure regions

Create an evidence matrix crossing workload, stressor, and metric. For each configuration, record throughput or goodput, p50/p95/p99 latency where sample size supports them, memory, movement/transfer volume, quality, and failure outcomes. Add ablations that remove the mechanism's key ingredient. Include at least one regime where the proposal should lose: rapid phase changes, low draft acceptance, tiny requests, very slow links, or visually ambiguous scenes. A method with an explained failure boundary is more useful than one evaluated only on favorable conditions.

## Write and defend a reproducible claim

The technical report should let a reader reconstruct the argument without browsing your chat history. Start with the concrete problem and result scope. Explain the baseline's bottleneck using a timeline or cost model, present the intervention and invariants, describe the experimental setup, then show results and competing explanations. Include a limitations section that states what was not measured. Use confidence labels deliberately: high for reproduced arithmetic and validated invariants, moderate for effects supported by repeated experiments on limited hardware, and unknown for untested deployment-scale generalization.

Package the repository so an outsider can reproduce a small result quickly. Provide a smoke command, a full evaluation command, estimated runtime and hardware requirements, pinned dependencies, raw results, plotting code, and checkpoint/data provenance. Avoid publishing private input traces; create a documented synthetic generator or redistributable subset with comparable workload statistics. Follow the [OSDI artifact guidance](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi24/call-for-artifacts) as a practical standard. For a DeepInfer-inspired project, cite the exact [source snapshot](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepInfer/tree/9bd9cf243fc53ef9afbf8f04d391d989117d6ab9) and identify which production components were outside your reproduction.

Your oral defense is five minutes: state the claim, derive why it should work, show the strongest evidence, explain the strongest counterexample, and name the next experiment that could overturn your conclusion. Passing requires a reviewer to understand both the contribution and its limits. The course ends when you can reason this way independently; frontier work continues through better questions, stronger baselines, and repeated contact with real workloads.

exercises.title: Make a vague claim falsifiable
exercises.prompt: Rewrite “adaptive speculation is faster” as a testable capstone hypothesis with a predicted failure region.
exercises.hint: Specify workload, resources, objective, intervention, and comparison.
exercises.solution: Example: On fixed hardware and a held-out mixed-code/chat trace at matched offered load, an occupancy-aware draft-length controller improves SLO goodput over the best fixed draft length at equal quality and memory budget. Predict little benefit on stationary low-occupancy traffic and possible losses when controller overhead exceeds saved verification work. Fix thresholds and tuning budgets before testing.

exercises.title: Calculate a conservative migration gate
exercises.prompt: A move costs 90 ms, saves an estimated 0.4 ms/step, and requires a 30 ms uncertainty margin. What horizon justifies migration? What if the phase lasts 200 steps?
exercises.hint: Compare H×0.4 against 90+30.
exercises.solution: Require H>300 useful steps. At 200 steps, predicted savings are 80 ms, below even the 90 ms raw cost, and 40 ms below the conservative threshold. The policy should not migrate under these assumptions.

exercises.title: Defend a negative result
exercises.prompt: Your adaptive policy never beats a strong fixed baseline. Design a report that still establishes something useful.
exercises.hint: Rule out implementation bugs and identify the missing opportunity.
exercises.solution: Verify correctness, equal tuning and resources, and controller overhead. Compare to an oracle to measure possible headroom. If even the oracle barely helps, the workload offers little adaptation opportunity. If the oracle helps strongly, diagnose estimation delay or migration cost. Publish raw results, failure boundaries, and the specific conclusion supported; do not invent novelty or hide the baseline.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest capstone claim?
options: Our system is state of the art
A specified mechanism improves a declared metric on matched held-out workloads with measured limits
quiz.explanation: A useful research claim specifies the intervention, comparison, workload, metric, and limits. That structure makes it possible to reproduce the result and identify evidence that would falsify it.

quiz.question: What role should a future-aware oracle play?
options: A source of hidden test tuning
Proof that your controller is optimal
quiz.explanation: An oracle with future knowledge can estimate remaining opportunity, but its information advantage is not available to a deployable controller. Label it separately and compare practical methods under matched information.

quiz.question: When can a negative result be a successful capstone?
options: When the baseline was intentionally weak
When controlled evidence explains a mechanism’s limits and rules out obvious confounders
quiz.explanation: A controlled negative result can show that a plausible mechanism has little headroom or fails for a specific reason. Strong baselines, correctness checks, and ruled-out confounders make that boundary useful evidence.

quiz.question: A CPU simulation improves predicted work by 15%. What can you claim?
options: The specified model objective improved 15% under the simulated assumptions
quiz.explanation: The observed result concerns the simulator’s objective and assumptions. Accelerator latency, network behavior, and production cost require additional measurements and cannot inherit the same percentage automatically.

quiz.question: What should the final defense name besides its strongest result?
options: The strongest counterexample and next falsifying experiment
An unmeasured scaling estimate as fact
quiz.explanation: A research defense must show where the method fails and which next experiment could overturn its explanation. Those boundaries make the claim usable and testable instead of merely persuasive.
